# 4 Maccabees Chapter 2 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Reason's Rule Over the Passions

---

**1** So if reason can govern the passions that get in the way of justice — things like greed and desire — then it can certainly also govern the passions that stand against courage: anger, pain, and fear.

**2** How does reason master greed? When a person lives by the law, even if they are naturally greedy, the law compels them to lend money without charging interest to those in need, and to cancel debts in the jubilee year.

**3** If someone is greedy, reason, working through the law, overcomes that greed — so that they do not strip their fields clean or harvest every last grape from their vineyard. You can see this principle at work in every area of life.

**4** The law even overrides natural love for one's parents — virtue cannot be compromised for their sake.

**5** It overrides love for a spouse — a husband must reprove his wife when she does wrong.

**6** It overrides love for one's children — they must be disciplined when they go astray.

**7** It overrides the bonds of friendship — a friend must be rebuked when acting wickedly.

**8** And do not think it strange that reason, through the law, can even master hatred toward enemies — for the law forbids cutting down an enemy's fruit trees and requires protecting an enemy's property from looters.

**9** Reason also reins in the more powerful passions: the craving for power, vanity, boasting, arrogance, and spite.

**10** The disciplined mind pushes back against all these destructive impulses — just as it does with anger.

**11** Consider Moses: when he was furious with Dathan and Abiram, he did not act out of anger. He governed his rage with reason.

**12** As I said, the disciplined mind can get the better of the passions — redirecting some, disarming others.

**13** Why else did wise Jacob rebuke Simeon and Levi for brutally wiping out the whole people of Shechem? He said, 'Cursed be their anger.'

**14** If reason had no power to restrain anger, he would never have said that.

**15** When God created human beings, he built our emotions and our moral instincts into us.

**16** But he also set the mind as a sacred governor over all those drives, ruling through the senses.

**17** He gave the mind the law — and the person who lives by the law will govern themselves with self-control, justice, goodness, and courage.

**18** But someone might ask: if reason is master of the passions, why doesn't it master forgetfulness and ignorance too?

**19** That argument is absurd. Reason is not the master of its own limitations — it is the master of the passions that oppose justice, courage, self-control, and wisdom. And over those it rules — not by destroying them, but by refusing to surrender to them.

**20** I could show you through countless examples that reason really does govern the passions.

**21** Fire blazes with tremendous heat, but water quickly puts it out. In the same way, even the most intense passion is quenched by the rational mind.

**22** You can see this in many places, but most powerfully in the life and death of Eleazar.

**23** While he was being tortured — fire still blazing, blood still flowing — he endured that terrible suffering with unwavering composure.
